finding.claim: Authorization bypass: the error returned by Authorize is discarded in dropTable, so any authenticated user, with or without the 'dba' role, can run the privileged DROP TABLE operation.
finding.source: Any authenticated HTTP client lacking the 'dba' role sends a request to /admin/drop.

trace.note: Authorize(u, "dba") returns an error for non-dba users, but the result is ignored

finding.guards_checked: Compared with vacuum (api.go:33-36), which checks the error and returns 403. dropTable has no check. No middleware is registered in main (api.go:43-46). userFrom (api.go:22) only retrieves the user from the context and does not enforce roles.

verdict.guard_found: none effective. Authorize (api.go:13-20) returns an error, but dropTable's call at api.go:26 is a bare statement that discards it. No middleware is registered (api.go:43-46). userFrom (api.go:22) only reads the context.
verdict.reason: api.go:26 discards the error from Authorize(u, "dba"), so runSQL("DROP TABLE "+r.FormValue("t")) at api.go:27 runs for any caller that userFrom can resolve; the checked version at api.go:33 shows the intended guard. Caveat: this file never sets the "user" context value, so the unchecked type assertion at api.go:22 would panic here. The bypass therefore depends on an out-of-repo authentication layer populating the context, and the finding assumes that layer exists.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Authorize (api.go:13-20) returns an error for non-dba users, but dropTable calls it as a bare statement at api.go:26. No middleware is registered in main (api.go:43-46).
verdict_facts.reason: api.go:26 discards Authorize's error, so api.go:27 runs DROP TABLE with the user-supplied table name for any authenticated user. The sibling vacuum handler checks the error at api.go:33-36, which confirms the check is meant to be there.

finding.claim: SQL injection: the table name from the request parameter 't' is concatenated directly into a DROP TABLE statement without validation or quoting, so a caller can inject arbitrary SQL, for example 't=x; DROP TABLE users' or a different table name.
finding.source: r.FormValue("t"), a query or form parameter controlled by the requester.

trace.note: r.FormValue("t") is concatenated into the SQL string and passed to runSQL
runSQL is a stub here but is the SQL execution sink

finding.guards_checked: No identifier allowlist, regex validation or quoting. The only gate is Authorize, which is ineffective (F1). Identifiers cannot be bound as parameters, so an allowlist is required.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 — its error return is discarded, so it never blocks. No allowlist, quoting, or parameterization on the table name.
verdict.reason: api.go:27 concatenates r.FormValue("t") into "DROP TABLE " and passes it to runSQL (api.go:41, a stub sink), and the only guard, Authorize at api.go:26, is a bare call whose error is ignored (unlike vacuum at api.go:33), so any authenticated user can reach it with arbitrary table names or injected SQL.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 is a bare statement whose error is discarded, so it blocks nothing. There is no allowlist, quoting or parameterization on the table name.
verdict_facts.reason: api.go:27 concatenates r.FormValue("t") into "DROP TABLE " and passes it to runSQL, and the only guard, Authorize at api.go:26, has its returned error ignored (unlike vacuum at api.go:33), so any authenticated user can reach it.

finding.claim: Unchecked type assertion on the context value: if the 'user' key is missing (unauthenticated request or no auth middleware), r.Context().Value("user").(*User) panics. This is a robustness and availability issue. net/http recovers per-request panics, so the impact is limited. A plain string context key also risks collisions.
finding.source: An unauthenticated request, since no middleware sets the context value in this code.
finding.sink: The type assertion at api.go:22, called from both handlers.

trace.note: Value("user") returns nil and the single-value assertion to *User panics

finding.guards_checked: No auth middleware is present in main. net/http recovers the panic, so the server does not crash. Authentication is also not enforced anywhere in this file.

verdict.guard_found: none that prevents the panic; net/http's per-request recover only contains it. No middleware in main (api.go:43-47) sets "user" and there is no comma-ok check at api.go:22.
verdict.reason: api.go:22 uses a single-value assertion `.(*User)` on `Value("user")`, and nothing in api.go:43-47 sets that key, so any anonymous request to the handlers at api.go:25 or api.go:32 panics; net/http recovers it per request, so this is a low-severity robustness issue rather than a crash or bypass. Separately, api.go:26 discards the result of `Authorize` and api.go:27 builds SQL from `r.FormValue("t")`. Those are distinct findings, and they are not reachable today only because the panic at line 22 always fires first.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Trusted upstream middleware populates the "user" context value (per project facts). Even if it were missing, net/http recovers the per-request panic, so the request fails closed.
verdict_facts.reason: The lines at api.go:22, 25 and 32 are accurately described, but the assertion at api.go:22 only panics if upstream middleware fails to set the user. A panic there is recovered per request and fails closed before runSQL, so it gives an attacker no security impact beyond a robustness nit.
